title: Counting
hook: an old method: count breaths from one to ten, then begin again

segments.voice: Yesterday, watching change: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go. Your line was let go. What ending did you notice? Day one hundred and fourteen.

Sometimes it goes like this. You sit down to watch the breath. Three breaths in, you're planning dinner. Then you're rehearsing an argument. Then you're wondering if you left the stove on. Five minutes later you remember: oh, right, the breath. Sixteen beautiful steps are no use if you can't stay for two. So the old teachers gave beginners something simpler to hold on to. Something any child can do. They count.
screen: `THREE BREATHS, THEN DINNER PLANS.` → `OH, RIGHT, THE BREATH.` → `SOMETHING SIMPLER: COUNT.`

segments.voice: The method is described in the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, as the very first stage of breath meditation for a beginner: ganana, counting. Breathe in, breathe out: one. Breathe in, breathe out: two. Up to ten. Then back to one. And if you lose count, which you will, you also go back to one. The manual is oddly specific about the numbers. Don't stop below five, it says, and don't go beyond ten. Why? If you only count to three or four, the mind feels cramped and restless, like cattle shut in a pen that's too small. If you count past ten, the mind starts paying attention to the numbers instead of the breath. Five to ten is the sweet spot: long enough to settle, short enough to stay with. The manual also says that once the mind can stay with the breath without the counting, you let the counting go. It's scaffolding, not the building. Counting isn't found only in this one manual; some Zen and Tibetan teachers count breaths with beginners too. Here's the part that matters most. Losing count isn't failure. It's the practice. Every time you notice you've drifted off to dinner plans and go back to one, that noticing is the muscle getting stronger. Reaching ten isn't the goal, and missing it isn't a mark against you. Whatever happens, the instruction stays the same, with no scolding at all. Back to one.
screen: `ONE TO TEN, THEN BEGIN AGAIN.` · `NOT BELOW FIVE, NOT PAST TEN.` · `SCAFFOLDING, NOT THE BUILDING.` · `LOSING COUNT IS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `BACK TO ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be natural. After each out-breath, count silently: one. Next out-breath: two. Continue to ten, then begin again at one. If you lose track, or catch yourself at fourteen, just smile, and go back to one. No judgment. Try for three rounds, if the time allows; if you only reach three, that's fine too. The counting is a handrail. Keep one hand on it. The bell holds the time.
Counting. An old method for a wandering mind: count breaths from one to ten, and begin again.
Your line: back to one. Today, whenever you lose your place, in a task, a conversation, a plan, say it kindly to yourself: back to one. Day one hundred and fourteen.

howItsDone: Counting breaths from one to ten is a beginner's method described in the Visuddhimagga and also used by some Zen and Tibetan teachers, with the instruction to begin again at one whenever the count is lost.

trapdoor: what you thought: counting sheep for grown-ups.
what it means: a handrail for a wandering mind, dropped once the mind can stay with the breath.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga VIII lists eight stages of breath practice, beginning with ganana (counting) and anubandhana (connection, following the breath).

notes: The Visuddhimagga's 'not below five, not beyond ten' rule and the cattle-pen image are paraphrased; confirm.
The Visuddhimagga counts at the in- or out-breath in different ways (slow and fast counting); the practice simplifies to counting after each out-breath.
The eight stages in the trapdoor (counting, connection, contact, fixing, observing, turning away, purification, looking back) should be checked.
Zen and Tibetan use of counting is mentioned briefly as shared practice within Buddhism.
